title: The False Consensus Effect: An Egocentric Bias in Social Perception and Attribution Processes

source.title: The False Consensus Effect: An Egocentric Bias in Social Perception and Attribution Processes
source.authors: Lee Ross, David Greene, Pamela House

studies.title: Study 1: Hypothetical stories, consensus estimates and trait ratings
studies.description: Questionnaire study. Each participant read one of four brief stories, estimated peer consensus for two options, indicated their own choice and rated a typical person who would choose each option.

studies.title: Study 2: Personal description items and perceived commonness
studies.description: Questionnaire study. Participants categorised themselves on 35 person description items and estimated the percentage of college students in general in each category (34 items analysed).

studies.title: Study 3: Hypothetical sandwich-board conflict
studies.description: Questionnaire study. Participants read a hypothetical request to wear a sandwich board sign, indicated their own choice, estimated peer consensus and rated typical individuals who agreed or refused.

studies.title: Study 4: Real sandwich-board conflict
studies.description: Field study. Participants were actually asked to wear a sandwich board sign, made a private choice, estimated peer consensus and rated two supposedly real previous participants.

nodes.title: Paper overview
nodes.summary: Four studies on the false consensus effect: raters’ own choices bias their estimates of peer consensus and their trait inferences about actors.

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Questionnaire studies (Studies 1–3) and one authentic conflict field study (Study 4)

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Evidence from four studies demonstrates that social observers tend to perceive a “false consensus” with respect to the relative commonness of their own responses.

nodes.title: Hypothesis 1: own choice and perceived consensus

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Subjects who “choose” a particular hypothetical response will rate that response as more probable for “people in general” than will subjects who “choose” the alternative response.

nodes.title: Hypothesis 2: own choice and trait inference

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Subjects who “choose” a specified response will use less extreme and less confident trait ratings in characterizing a “typical” person making that response than will subjects who “choose” the alternative response.

nodes.title: Finding: own choices bias perceived consensus and trait inference

fields.label: Answer
fields.value: Raters’ perceptions of consensus and their trait inferences reflect their own behavioural choices across questionnaire and authentic conflict situations.

nodes.title: Validity and limitations reported by the authors

fields.label: Limitations
fields.value: Trait-rating effects were not independent of consensus estimates; covariance analyses reduced the F ratios and the effect was no longer significant for most stories and both final studies.

issues.title: Study 3 assignment to sign version
issues.reason: The paper says subjects read one of two versions but does not state how versions were assigned.
issues.impact: Condition sample sizes cannot be replayed without a rule.
issues.suggestedAction: Researcher to supply the assignment rule or confirm it was unspecified.

issues.title: Study 3 trait scale anchors
issues.reason: The paper states the scales were essentially similar to Study 1 and lists the eight traits, but does not print the anchors.

issues.title: Study 4 experimenter script
issues.reason: The paper gives a slightly expanded version of the experimenter script rather than the full wording.
issues.impact: Verbatim replay of the field request is incomplete.
issues.suggestedAction: Researcher to supply the exact script if available.

issues.title: Study 1 questionnaire order
issues.reason: The order of the three rating sheets was systematically varied; the order rule is not described further.
issues.impact: Replay order of sheets is not fixed by the paper.
issues.suggestedAction: Keep order as a counterbalanced factor.

issues.title: Study 2 test statistic
issues.reason: The item-wise significance is reported but the test statistic per item is not restated in the text.
issues.impact: Analysis step cannot be fully specified.
